post.description: A delivery worker receives one body-bound, tenant-derived capability.

Issue the ``smr-worker-host`` capability for one run's control RPC.

An SMR runtime host drives its own control plane (tick flush, runtime
wakeup) over the same HTTP surface the backend uses, and it was minting the
capability for that call in-process. A runtime holds no signing key, so
every wakeup failed reporting a missing secret; restoring the key there
would have made a verifier a second issuer.

The ``worker_id`` claim names the host that will *receive* the RPC and is
resolved here, by the same resolver the backend uses for its own control
calls, from the caller's own run. It is never taken from the request: a
caller that could name its own callee could address another pool's runtime.
post.summary: Issue Run Control Capability For Runtime

post.description:
Issue a run's MQ capability to the host that owns that run.

``/mq-orchestrate`` is the cross-tenant authority: the temporal-worker
orchestrates every tenant's runs, so it authenticates a cross-tenant `mq`
service key and derives the org from durable bindings. An SMR runtime host
needs far less than that -- it creates and reads the threads of the runs
dispatched to *its own pool* -- and the cross-tenant key is not provisioned
on a runtime, so the runtime fell through to an in-process mint it has no
signing key for.

This is that narrower authority. The caller must prove it owns the run
(``app.auth.run_authority``), and the org comes from the run's own row, so
this cannot reach another tenant even by mistake. A thread-less run is
genuine provisioning and mints the org-scoped token thread creation needs;
once a thread exists the grant is attenuated to it, exactly as the
cross-tenant issuer does (and with the same ``mint_mq_jwt`` scopes).

Issue a run-scoped capability to the SMR runtime host that owns the run.

Authority chain, all of it server-side: the caller's enrolled key names a
dispatch pool; the run names the pool it was dispatched to; the two must be
the same, the run must belong to the key's tenant (a platform key serves
any tenant; the tenant is then read from the run row), and it must still be
live. Nothing in the request body contributes to the issued claims except
which run and which audience -- the org and the project are read from the
run row, so a caller cannot widen its own grant.
post.summary: Issue Run Service Capability For Runtime

post.description:
Prove that a pool runtime can reach its issuer and verify its output.

This exchange is deliberately run-independent and grants no run or project
authority. The runtime verifies the returned token with its configured
public key set before it advertises capacity, catching missing enrollment,
issuer routing, signer publication, and verifier trust without launching a
paid actor.

post.description:
Responses in, Responses out -- proxied natively, never bridged.

Codex speaks only the Responses wire. Round-tripping it through Chat
Completions is lossy in a way that is invisible at the HTTP layer: the chat
wire has no representation for a Responses ``function_call`` item, so an
agent's tool calls are dropped, it answers in prose, executes nothing, and
the rollout scores badly as though the model were weak.

So this proxies to the provider's own ``/responses`` endpoint and returns
what it says. A provider without one is refused explicitly rather than
bridged, because a clear 502 beats a silently degraded agent.
